Mahath
MAY-hath
n. (proper, a Kohathite Levite; Hebrew, a snatching away)
Hebrew Machath, probably a grasping or a snatching away. Two Levites bear it: one in Samuel's ancestral line, and one who is named first among the Levites who arose at Hezekiah's call to cleanse the house of the LORD.

Biblical Definition

He stands in the pedigree that runs up to Samuel the prophet: “The son of Zuph, the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai” (1 Chronicles 6:35). The great scene is Hezekiah's reformation. The king opened the doors of the house of the LORD in the first month of his reign, gathered the Levites and charged them to sanctify themselves and carry out the filthiness from the holy place, and the response is recorded name by name: “Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi” (2 Chronicles 29:12). His name comes first in the list of those who arose. Later, when the tithes came in and had to be handled honestly, he is among those appointed: “Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah” (2 Chronicles 31:13).

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Kohathite Levite in Samuel's line, and one who arose first at Hezekiah's call to cleanse the temple.

expand to see more

KOHATHITE, n. A descendant of Kohath the son of Levi; the division of Levites charged with the holiest vessels.

CLEANSE, v.t. To purify; to make clean; to remove filth or foul matter of any kind.

OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a supervisor; one who has the care of others.

REFORMATION, n. Change from worse to better; amendment of life, manners, or of anything vicious or corrupt.

TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy.

Key Scripture

1 Chronicles 6:35 — "The son of Zuph, the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai,"

2 Chronicles 29:12 — "Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehalelel: and of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah:"

2 Chronicles 31:13 — "And Jehiel, and Azaziah, and Nahath, and Asahel, and Jerimoth, and Jozabad, and Eliel, and Ismachiah, and Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king, and Azariah the ruler of the house of God."

2 Chronicles 29:5 — "And said unto them, Hear me, ye Levites, sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the LORD God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place."

Modern Corruption

Reformation is imagined as a change of preaching that leaves the practical house untouched; Hezekiah's began with Levites carrying filth out of the holy place, and continued with honest men set over the tithes.

expand to see more

2 Chronicles 29 shows what a reformation actually costs in labour. Hezekiah's charge was blunt: Sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the LORD God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place. The doors had been shut, the lamps put out, the incense unoffered. The first act of renewal was manual: named men, Mahath at the head of them, carrying rubbish out of a building. Sixteen days of it before a sacrifice could be offered. Renewal that never reaches the actual state of the house is sentiment, and Scripture measures it by what gets carried out.

The second stage is just as practical and more easily neglected. When the reformation succeeded, the people brought tithes in heaps, and the immediate problem was administration — and 2 Chronicles 31 lists by name the overseers set over the store, Mahath among them, under Cononiah and his brother. Revival produces resources, and resources require accountable men. A movement that will not appoint overseers over its heaps is preparing its own scandal, and the chronicler thought the names of the men who handled the money worth recording.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Machath (H4287), a snatching away; Qehath (H6955), Kohath; qadash (H6942), to sanctify; niddah (H5079), filthiness or impurity.

expand to see more

Hebrew Machath (H4287) — Mahath; probably a grasping or snatching away.

Hebrew Qehath (H6955) — Kohath; the Levitical division charged with the holy vessels.

Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to set apart, to sanctify; sanctify now yourselves.

Hebrew niddah (H5079) — impurity, filthiness; what was carried out of the holy place.

Hebrew paqiyd (H6496) — an overseer, an appointed officer; his later charge.

Usage

"“Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai” — named first."

"“Carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place” — the first labour."

"“Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers” — accountable men over the heaps."
